description_full: Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV produces and sells beer in North America, Middle Americas, South America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. It operates through North America, Middle Americas, South America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, and Global Export and Holding Companies segments. The company also offers flavored malt beverages, soft drinks, spirit-based ready-to-drink cocktails and beverages, and energy drinks. In addition, it operates BEES, a business-to-business digital commerce platform; on-demand delivery platforms under the Zé Delivery and TaDa Delivery brands; and premium at-home draft system under the PerfectDraft brand. The company provides a portfolio of approximately 500 beer brands, which primarily include Budweiser, Corona Extra, Michelob Ultra, and Stella Artois; Aguila, Brahma, Carling Black Label, Cass Fresh, Jupiler, Quilmes, SKOL, and Victoria; Beck's, Hoegaarden, and Leffe; Antarctica, Bud Light, Castle, Castle Lite, Cristal, Harbin, Modelo Especial, Sedrin, and Skol brands, as well as non-beer brands comprising Brutal Fruit, Cutwater, and NÜTRL brands. The company was formerly known as InBev SA and changed its name to Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV in November 2008. Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV was founded in 1366 and is headquartered in Leuven, Belgium.

financial_summary: Anheuser-Busch Inbev SA Sponsor is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $165.3B market cap on $59.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 16% against a 7% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 57% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $11.2B in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.76× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.9× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 3.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.

val: The stock trades 53% below its DCF fair value of $180, a meaningful margin of safety.

Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $94.53 on average, 13% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.46).
It runs a 57% gross margin and converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.

ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.9x net debt to EBITDA ($11.6B of cash against $73.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 3.0x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.53 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.72 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 54% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.9% over 3 years and 4.8% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.6% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 6.2% on average.
Analysts expect 10.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 6%.
It returns 4.0% a year to shareholders (1.4% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 16 consecutive years, raising it 17.4% a year over the last five.
